quizName: DMV Practice Test #12 40 Questions • Passing Score 32

questions.question: If hazards are on your left, where should you ride?

options.text: In the left portion of the lane.
In the right portion of the lane.
In any portion of the lane.
On the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the right portion of the lane.
questions.explanation: When hazards are on your left, ride in the right portion of the lane. Change your position as road and traffic conditions change.

questions.question: When riding with a passenger, what should you do?

options.text: Maintain your usual space cushion.
Brake later than usual.
Ride a little more slowly than usual.
Ride a little faster than usual.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride a little more slowly than usual.
questions.explanation: Your motorcycle sits lower with a passenger's weight. Ride slower than usual, especially on curves and bumps. The extra weight means longer stopping distance, so keep more distance between you and other vehicles.

questions.question: What type of clothing material offers the best protection for motorcyclists?

options.text: Leather
Wool
Polyester
Silk

questions.correctAnswerText: Leather
questions.explanation: Leather provides the best protection for motorcyclists. Always wear clothing that covers your legs and arms completely.

questions.question: What should you do when riding at night?

options.text: Be flexible about your lane position and adjust to changing conditions.
Travel faster than usual to reach your destination quickly.
Always use your low beam headlight to see better.
Stay close behind the vehicle ahead.

questions.correctAnswerText: Be flexible about your lane position and adjust to changing conditions.
questions.explanation: Be flexible about your lane position when riding at night. Use safe riding strategies in less than ideal conditions.

questions.question: If your motorcycle begins to wobble, what should you do?

options.text: Keep riding, as the wobble will likely correct itself.
Brake quickly.
Close the throttle to slow down.
Accelerate quickly.

questions.correctAnswerText: Close the throttle to slow down.
questions.explanation: Do not accelerate when your motorcycle wobbles. Grip the handlebars firmly and close the throttle slowly. Move your weight forward and down. Pull off the road and fix the problem.

questions.question: Does making eye contact with a driver guarantee they see you?

options.text: Yes, it means they see you.
Yes, they will yield to you.
No, it doesn't mean they see you.
No, it's not worth the effort.

questions.correctAnswerText: No, it doesn't mean they see you.
questions.explanation: Do not rely on eye contact. Drivers may look directly at you and still not notice you.

questions.question: What should you do before riding an unfamiliar motorcycle?

options.text: Ride it like your own bike since all bikes are the same.
Check the controls and shift pattern.
Trust the owner that everything works.
Assume you know where all controls are.

questions.correctAnswerText: Check the controls and shift pattern.
questions.explanation: All motorcycles are different. Check the controls and gear pattern before riding. Work the throttle, clutch, and brakes a few times first.

questions.question: When a group of riders passes another vehicle, how should they pass?

options.text: In a staggered formation.
In a pyramid formation.
One at a time.
In a splintered formation.

questions.correctAnswerText: One at a time.
questions.explanation: On a two-lane highway, riders should pass one at a time. The second rider waits until the first rider safely returns to the original lane before passing. Repeat this pattern until all riders have passed.

questions.question: Why should you check your motorcycle before riding?

options.text: Only a mechanic can do a useful check.
You shouldn't check before a ride.
You should only check after a ride.
It helps find mechanical problems or broken equipment.

questions.correctAnswerText: It helps find mechanical problems or broken equipment.
questions.explanation: Check your motorcycle thoroughly before every ride. This helps you find problems that could be dangerous.

questions.question: More than half of all motorcycle crashes involve:

options.text: Riding at night.
Bald tires.
Speeds above 55 mph.
Inexperienced riders.

questions.correctAnswerText: Inexperienced riders.
questions.explanation: More than half of crashes involve riders with less than six months of experience. Most crashes happen during the day at low speeds.

questions.question: A good lane position helps you do all of the following, except:

options.text: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots.
See better and be seen better.
Go faster.
Prepare for turns.

questions.correctAnswerText: Go faster.
questions.explanation: Your lane position affects your safety. It should help you see better and be seen better. It should also help you stay out of other drivers' blind spots and prepare you for turns.

questions.question: To stop quickly, you should:

options.text: Release the throttle and use the front brake.
Use the rear brake only.
Use the front brake only.
Use both brakes at the same time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both brakes at the same time.
questions.explanation: To stop quickly, use both brakes at the same time.

questions.question: Your lane position should do all of the following, except:

options.text: Help you avoid road hazards.
Help you stay out of other drivers' blind spots.
Help you avoid being seen by other drivers.
Help other drivers see you better.

questions.correctAnswerText: Help you avoid being seen by other drivers.
questions.explanation: A good lane position should help you see and be seen better. It should keep you out of other drivers' blind spots and help you avoid road hazards. It should also protect you from wind blasts and give you an escape route from hazards.

questions.question: When braking on a slippery surface, you should:

options.text: Brake faster than normal.
Brake slower and more gently than normal.
Not use the rear brake.
Not use the front brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brake slower and more gently than normal.
questions.explanation: On a slippery surface, brake gently and carefully. This will help prevent skidding.

questions.question: When passing parked cars on your right with no oncoming traffic, you should:

options.text: Stay toward the right side of your lane.
Stay toward the left side of your lane.
Look to your left frequently.
Use your rearview mirrors more often than usual.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay toward the left side of your lane.
questions.explanation: When passing parked cars, stay on the side of your lane away from the cars. This protects you from car doors opening or people stepping out. This distance helps keep you safe.

questions.question: When securing a load on your motorcycle, place it:

options.text: As high as possible.
As low as possible.
On a sissy bar.
Only on one side of the motorcycle.

questions.correctAnswerText: As low as possible.
questions.explanation: Keep loads low and centered. Placing them too high, like on a sissy bar, raises the motorcycle's center of gravity and hurts balance. Spread loads evenly on both sides of the motorcycle.

questions.question: When stopping, you should:

options.text: Apply the rear brake first.
Apply the front brake first.
Apply both brakes at the same time.
Use only one brake, either front or rear.

questions.correctAnswerText: Apply both brakes at the same time.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes every time you slow down or stop. Apply them at the same time.

questions.question: Which of the following best protects your eyes from wind?

options.text: Eyeglasses
Sunglasses
A windshield
Goggles

questions.correctAnswerText: Goggles
questions.explanation: Goggles and face shields protect your eyes from wind. Most windshields, eyeglasses, and sunglasses do not provide adequate wind protection.

questions.question: When approaching railroad tracks that cross your lane at an angle, it is usually:

options.text: Safest to ride straight within your lane to cross the tracks.
Dangerous to ride straight within your lane to cross the tracks.
Not safe to cross tracks on a motorcycle.
Safest to cross the tracks on the road shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: Safest to ride straight within your lane to cross the tracks.
questions.explanation: When railroad tracks cross your lane at an angle, ride straight across them in your lane. Turning to cross at a 90-degree angle is dangerous because you could move into another lane of traffic.

questions.question: When slowing or stopping, you should use both brakes:

options.text: Only if the road is wet.
Not very often.
Only when riding in the city.
Every time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Every time.
questions.explanation: Using both brakes gives you the most stopping power. Use both brakes every time you slow down or stop.

questions.question: How can you tell if your rear tire is flat while riding?

options.text: You hear a hissing noise from the rear of the bike.
The back end jerks from side to side.
You cannot accelerate.
The rear brake stops working.

questions.correctAnswerText: The back end jerks from side to side.
questions.explanation: If your rear tire fails, the back of your motorcycle will jerk from side to side. You usually will not hear a tire fail while riding.

questions.question: A motorcycle with a sidecar:

options.text: Cannot tip over.
Can tip over if you turn too fast.
Can take corners at any speed.
Should not carry items.

questions.correctAnswerText: Can tip over if you turn too fast.
questions.explanation: Even with three wheels, a sidecar can tip over if you turn too sharply or go too fast around a corner.

questions.question: When braking, you should:

options.text: Squeeze the front brake lever and press the rear brake pedal.
Pull the front brake and squeeze the rear brake.
Jam the front brake and grab the rear brake.
Push down on the front brake and jam the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Squeeze the front brake lever and press the rear brake pedal.
questions.explanation: To brake, squeeze the front brake lever and press down on the rear brake pedal. Always use both brakes when slowing or stopping.

questions.question: Riding at night:

options.text: Is not recommended.
Is safer when you wear reflective clothing.
Is unsafe because other drivers cannot see your turn signals.
Should only be done in the city.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is safer when you wear reflective clothing.
questions.explanation: Wear reflective clothing when riding at night. This makes other drivers more likely to see you.

questions.question: When riding in a group, motorcyclists:

options.text: Do not need extra space around them.
Should increase their space around other riders.
Should cut their normal space in half.
Should keep enough space between riders.

questions.correctAnswerText: Should keep enough space between riders.
questions.explanation: When riding in a group, stay close together but keep enough space around each rider to stay safe.

questions.question: When carrying a passenger or cargo:

options.text: You accelerate slower but stop faster.
You accelerate slower and stop slower.
You accelerate slower but stop faster.
You accelerate faster and stop faster.

questions.correctAnswerText: You accelerate slower and stop slower.
questions.explanation: Extra weight slows down your motorcycle. It takes longer to speed up and longer to stop.

questions.question: When you park a motorcycle next to a curb, it should be:

options.text: Parked at a 90-degree angle with the rear wheel touching the curb.
Parked at a 45-degree angle with the front tire touching the curb.
Parked like a car, with both wheels the same distance from the curb.
Parked at the left side so drivers can see it better.

questions.correctAnswerText: Parked at a 90-degree angle with the rear wheel touching the curb.
questions.explanation: Park your motorcycle at a 90-degree angle to the curb with your rear wheel touching it.

questions.question: In a crash, you have a better chance of avoiding serious injury if you do all of the following, except:

options.text: Wear an approved helmet.
Wear face or eye protection.
Wear protective clothing.
Have a windshield.

questions.correctAnswerText: Have a windshield.
questions.explanation: Wear an approved helmet, face or eye protection, and protective clothing to reduce injury in a crash. A windshield does not protect you from injury.

questions.question: When checking tire pressure:

options.text: Looking at the tire is good enough.
Use a tire gauge.
Squeeze the tire to test it.
Compare the height of your tire to another tire.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use a tire gauge.
questions.explanation: Use a tire gauge to check your tire pressure before every ride. A tire can look fine but still be under-inflated.

questions.question: To lean a motorcycle when turning, you should:

options.text: Always press the left handgrip.
Always press the right handgrip.
Press the handgrip opposite the direction you are turning.
Press the handgrip in the direction you are turning.

questions.correctAnswerText: Press the handgrip in the direction you are turning.
questions.explanation: To turn, your motorcycle must lean. Press the handgrip in the direction you want to turn to make the motorcycle lean.

questions.question: What following distance should you normally keep between you and the vehicle ahead?

options.text: One second.
Two seconds.
Three seconds.
Four seconds.

questions.correctAnswerText: Two seconds.
questions.explanation: In normal conditions, keep at least two seconds of distance between you and the vehicle ahead. Increase this distance if weather or road conditions are poor.

questions.question: Why should you use your mirrors when stopped at an intersection?

options.text: To see if parked vehicles are entering traffic.
To look for vehicles changing lanes.
To watch for vehicles behind you that may not be slowing down.
To see if someone is planning to turn behind you.

questions.correctAnswerText: To watch for vehicles behind you that may not be slowing down.
questions.explanation: Check your mirrors at intersections to see cars coming from behind. They may not see you in time to stop, so you need to be ready to react.

questions.question: Who is most likely to have crashes?

options.text: Experienced riders.
Beginning riders.
Those familiar with their motorcycle.
Those who have completed a safety course.

questions.correctAnswerText: Beginning riders.
questions.explanation: New riders who lack training and are unfamiliar with their motorcycle are most likely to have crashes.

questions.question: Intersections are usually:

options.text: Safe because there is so much traffic.
A dangerous spot for riders.
Difficult to figure out.
Safer than the open road.

questions.correctAnswerText: A dangerous spot for riders.
questions.explanation: Intersections are dangerous because many conflicts can happen between motorcyclists and other drivers.

questions.question: If your motorcycle starts to wobble, what should you do?

options.text: Speed up to stop the wobble.
Brake immediately.
Grip the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle.
Downshift.

questions.correctAnswerText: Grip the handlebars firmly and slowly close the throttle.
questions.explanation: Do not speed up, as this makes the wobble worse. Instead, grip the handlebars tightly and slowly reduce speed. Lean forward and down. Pull off the road when safe. Do not use the brakes suddenly, as this can also worsen the wobble.

questions.question: When is it most important to flash your brake light?

options.text: When passing another vehicle.
When you will slow down suddenly.
When there is a stop sign ahead.
When your signals do not work.

questions.correctAnswerText: When you will slow down suddenly.
questions.explanation: A motorcycle's single brake light is harder to see than a car's two large brake lights. Flashing your brake light helps other drivers notice when you slow down quickly.

questions.question: If your motorcycle weaves while riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings, what should you do?

options.text: Brake suddenly.
Steer in a weaving pattern.
Relax, keep a steady speed, and ride straight across.
Move to the left side of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Relax, keep a steady speed, and ride straight across.
questions.explanation: Weaving over rain grooves or bridge gratings is usually not dangerous. Stay calm and continue straight at a steady speed. Trying to weave with the motorcycle will make things worse.

questions.question: What is true about passing in a no passing zone?

options.text: A motorcycle may still pass another vehicle.
A motorcycle is not allowed to pass another vehicle.
A motorcycle may pass if another vehicle is not coming.
A motorcycle may pass on the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: A motorcycle is not allowed to pass another vehicle.
questions.explanation: Passing is not allowed in no passing zones. You also cannot pass by riding off the main road.

questions.question: If using a sidecar to transport a load, what should you do?

options.text: Allow the load to move freely.
Secure the load so its weight does not shift.
Place the load unsecured in the seat.
Secure the load near the front of the sidecar.

questions.correctAnswerText: Secure the load so its weight does not shift.
questions.explanation: Secure loads in a sidecar so they do not move. Place the load toward the rear of the sidecar to prevent the sidecar from tipping up during sharp left turns.

questions.question: What type of sign is rectangular?

options.text: School crossing sign.
Railroad crossing sign.
Stop sign.
Speed limit sign.

questions.correctAnswerText: Speed limit sign.
questions.explanation: Regulatory signs, such as speed limit signs, are rectangular and white with black letters. You must follow the rules on these signs.
